messages.content:
Compute the largest positive integer \( n \) such that

\[
n \text{ divides } (\lfloor \sqrt{n} \rfloor)!^{n!} + 450.
\]

Put your final answer within \boxed{}.

message.content:
Let

\[
k=\lfloor \sqrt n\rfloor,\qquad A=k!,\qquad N=n!.
\]

We need

\[
n\mid A^N+450.
\]

We first make a useful observation about prime powers dividing \(n\).

Let \(p^a\) be a prime power dividing \(n\).

### Case 1: \(p\le k\)

Then \(p\mid k!\), so \(p\mid A\). Also, since \(p^a\mid n\), we have \(a\le n\), and therefore \(N=n!\ge a\). Hence

\[
v_p(A^N)=Nv_p(A)\ge N\ge a,
\]

so

\[
A^N\equiv 0\pmod{p^a}.
\]

Thus the divisibility condition forces

\[
p^a\mid 450.
\]

### Case 2: \(p>k\)

Then \(\gcd(A,p)=1\). Since \(p^a\mid n\), we have \(p^a\le n\). Also, for any prime power \(q=p^a\), Euler has \(\varphi(q)<q\). Therefore

\[
\varphi(p^a)<p^a\le n,
\]

so \(\varphi(p^a)\mid n!=N\). By Euler’s theorem,

\[
A^N\equiv 1\pmod{p^a}.
\]

Thus the divisibility condition forces

\[
p^a\mid 451.
\]

Now factor:

\[
450=2\cdot 3^2\cdot 5^2,\qquad 451=11\cdot 41.
\]

So every prime divisor of \(n\) must be one of

\[
2,3,5,11,41.
\]

Moreover:

- The \(2,3,5\)-part of \(n\) must divide \(450\).
- If \(11\mid n\), then necessarily \(11>k\), and \(11\) appears only to the first power.
- If \(41\mid n\), then necessarily \(41>k\), and \(41\) appears only to the first power.

Now we bound \(n\).

---

### Case A: \(41\mid n\)

Then \(41>k\), so \(k\le 40\), and therefore

\[
n\le 41^2-1=1680.
\]

Also, \(11\nmid n\): if \(11\mid n\) as well, then \(11>k\), so \(k\le 10\), giving \(n\le 120\), impossible since \(41\cdot 11=451>n\).

Thus \(n=41m\), where \(m\mid 450\). Since

\[
41m\le 1680,
\]

we get

\[
m\le 40.
\]

The largest divisor of \(450\) not exceeding \(40\) is \(30\). Hence

\[
n\le 41\cdot 30=1230.
\]

### Case B: \(41\nmid n\) but \(11\mid n\)

Then \(11>k\), so \(k\le 10\), and

\[
n\le 11^2-1=120.
\]

Write \(n=11m\), where \(m\mid 450\). Then

\[
m\le 10.
\]

The largest divisor of \(450\) not exceeding \(10\) is \(10\), so

\[
n\le 110.
\]

### Case C: Neither \(11\) nor \(41\) divides \(n\)

Then all prime factors of \(n\) lie in \(\{2,3,5\}\), and the whole number divides \(450\). Thus

\[
n\le 450.
\]

Therefore every valid \(n\) satisfies

\[
n\le 1230.
\]

It remains to check that \(n=1230\) actually works.

For \(n=1230\),

\[
\lfloor \sqrt{1230}\rfloor=35
\]

because

\[
35^2=1225<1230<1296=36^2.
\]

So \(A=35!\) and \(N=1230!\).

Modulo \(30\), since \(30\mid 35!\),

\[
(35!)^{1230!}\equiv 0\pmod{30},
\]

and \(450\equiv 0\pmod{30}\), so

\[
(35!)^{1230!}+450\equiv 0\pmod{30}.
\]

Modulo \(41\), since \(41\nmid 35!\) and \(40\mid 1230!\),

\[
(35!)^{1230!}\equiv 1\pmod{41}.
\]

Thus

\[
(35!)^{1230!}+450\equiv 1+450=451\equiv 0\pmod{41}.
\]

Since \(\gcd(30,41)=1\), we get

\[
1230\mid (35!)^{1230!}+450.
\]

Therefore the largest possible value is

\[
\boxed{1230}.
\]
